lead: The networking cert for every IT rating. It proves you can build, run, secure and troubleshoot the networks a unit lives on, and it sets you up for Security+ and CCNA.
planSub: Set how many hours a week you can give it. The plan splits about 100 hours across the domains by exam weight, then saves the last stretch for practice tests, subnetting drills and PBQs.

v9.label: V9
v9.note: The current version. CompTIA estimates it retires around 2027, three years after launch, so check the exam page before you book if you plan to test late that year.
v9.onote: Summary bullets from CompTIA's V9 page. The full objectives PDF breaks each domain into numbered sub-objectives.

domains.name: Networking Concepts
obj: Physical, data link, network, transport, session, presentation, application.
Routers, switches, firewalls, IDS/IPS, load balancers, proxies, NAS, SAN and wireless devices.
NFV, VPC, network security groups, cloud gateways, deployment models (public, private, hybrid) and service models (SaaS, IaaS, PaaS).
FTP, SFTP, SSH, Telnet, SMTP, DNS, DHCP, HTTP, HTTPS, SNMP, LDAP, RDP, SIP.
Wireless (802.11, cellular, satellite) and wired (fiber, coaxial, DAC).
SC, LC, ST, MPO, RJ11, RJ45, F-type, BNC.
Mesh, hybrid, star/hub-and-spoke, spine-and-leaf, point-to-point, three-tier, collapsed core.
Public vs. private, APIPA, RFC 1918, loopback, subnetting (VLSM, CIDR), address classes A–E.

domains.name: Network Implementation
obj: Static and dynamic routing (BGP, EIGRP, OSPF), route selection, NAT, PAT, FHRP, VIP, subinterfaces.
VLANs, interface configuration, spanning tree, MTU, jumbo frames.
Channels, frequency options, SSID, network types, encryption, guest networks, authentication, antennas, access points.
Installation implications, power considerations, environmental factors.

domains.name: Network Operations
obj: Physical vs. logical diagrams, rack diagrams, cable maps, asset inventory, IPAM, SLAs, wireless surveys.
SNMP, flow data, packet capture, baseline metrics, log aggregation, API integration, port mirroring.
RPO, RTO, MTTR, MTBF, cold/warm/hot sites, active-active/passive, testing.
DHCP, SLAAC, DNS, NTP, PTP, NTS.

domains.name: Network Security
obj: Encryption in transit and at rest, PKI, IAM, MFA, SSO, RADIUS, LDAP, SAML, TACACS+, least privilege, RBAC, geofencing.
Risk, vulnerability, exploit, threat, CIA triad.
IoT, IIoT, SCADA, ICS, OT, guest, BYOD.
DoS/DDoS, VLAN hopping, MAC flooding, ARP and DNS poisoning, rogue devices, evil twin, on-path, social engineering.
Device hardening, NAC, key management, ACLs, URL/content filtering, trusted vs. untrusted zones, screened subnet.

domains.name: Network Troubleshooting
obj: Identify the problem, establish a theory, test, plan and implement a solution, verify functionality, document findings.
Wrong cable type, signal degradation, bad termination, TX/RX transposed, rising counters, port status, PoE, transceiver mismatch, signal strength.
STP, VLAN assignment, ACLs, routing tables and default routes, address pool exhaustion, wrong gateway/IP/subnet mask.
Congestion, latency, packet loss, wireless interference.
Protocol analyzers, command-line tools, cable testers, Wi-Fi analyzers.

extras.title: OSI model
rows: HTTP, DNS, SMTP: what the user's app talks

method: Use the domains above as your checklist. Troubleshooting and Networking Concepts carry almost half the exam.
Pick one video course and finish it end to end. Draw the diagrams yourself as you go.
Build networks in Cisco Packet Tracer, capture traffic in Wireshark, and run ipconfig, ping, tracert and nslookup until they're second nature.
Drill subnetting every day until a /26 to /30 takes under a minute. Flashcards for ports and the OSI layers.
Timed practice exams. Review every miss. A common target is 85%+ twice in a row before you book.
tips: They often come first and eat time. Flag them, finish the multiple choice, then come back.
Write your subnet table on the whiteboard or scratch sheet as soon as the exam starts.
BEST, FIRST and MOST change the answer. Several options can be true; only one fits.
There is no penalty for a wrong answer, so always pick something.

quiz.q: A network admin needs at least 50 usable host addresses per subnet and wants to waste as few addresses as possible. Which prefix length should they use?
o: Right. A /26 gives 64 addresses, 62 of them usable: enough for 50 with the least waste.
A /27 has only 30 usable hosts, which is too few.
A /25 gives 126 usable hosts. It works, but wastes far more addresses than needed.
A /24 gives 254 usable hosts, the most wasteful of the options that work.

quiz.q: A device makes forwarding decisions using MAC addresses and builds a table of which MAC lives on which port. At which OSI layer does it primarily work?
o: Layer 2, data link
Right. That's a switch: it forwards frames by MAC address using its MAC (CAM) table.
Layer 1, physical
Layer 1 devices like hubs just repeat signals. They don't read addresses at all.
Layer 3, network
Layer 3 devices like routers forward by IP address, not MAC address.
Layer 4, transport
Layer 4 deals with TCP/UDP ports and segments, not frame forwarding.

quiz.q: A router has two routes that cover 10.20.30.15: an OSPF route to 10.20.0.0/16 and a static route to 10.20.30.0/24. Which route carries the packet, and why?
o: The static /24 route, because it's the most specific match
Right. Routers use longest prefix match first. A /24 beats a /16, whatever the route source.
The static /24 route, because static routes always win on administrative distance
Same route, wrong reason. Administrative distance only breaks ties between routes with the SAME prefix length.
The OSPF /16 route, because dynamic routes adapt to changes
Being dynamic doesn't give a route priority. The more specific /24 wins.
The default route, because two routes conflict
There's no conflict to resolve. Both routes are valid, and the most specific one is used.

quiz.q: Users on VLAN 10 and VLAN 20 plug into the same switch. Each group reaches its own VLAN fine, but the two VLANs can't talk to each other. What is needed?
o: A Layer 3 device to route between the VLANs
Right. VLANs are separate broadcast domains. A router (router-on-a-stick) or a Layer 3 switch has to route between them.
Enable spanning tree on the switch
STP prevents loops. It doesn't let separate VLANs reach each other.
Set both VLANs as the native VLAN
Only one native VLAN exists per trunk, and that wouldn't route traffic between VLANs anyway.
Turn on jumbo frames
Jumbo frames change the frame size (MTU). They have nothing to do with inter-VLAN traffic.

quiz.q: An organization runs two data centers that both serve live traffic. If one fails, the other carries the full load with no switchover delay. Which design is this?
o: Active-active
Right. Both sites handle traffic at the same time, so losing one only means more load on the other.
Active-passive
In active-passive, the standby site sits idle until a failover happens.
Hot site
A hot site is a fully equipped standby location. It isn't carrying live traffic during normal operations.
Warm site
A warm site has equipment but needs data and configuration work before it can take over.

quiz.q: An analyst needs a copy of every packet going to and from a server so they can analyze it in Wireshark, without adding any inline hardware. What should be configured on the switch?
o: Port mirroring (SPAN)
Right. Mirroring copies the server port's traffic to the analyst's port for full packet capture.
NetFlow
NetFlow exports summaries (who talked to whom, how much), not full packet contents.
SNMP traps
Traps are device alerts sent to a monitoring server. They don't carry user traffic.
Jumbo frames
Jumbo frames change frame size. They don't copy traffic anywhere.

quiz.q: An attacker sets up an access point broadcasting the same SSID as the base guest Wi-Fi, hoping users connect and type in their logins. What is this attack?
o: Evil twin
Right. An evil twin impersonates a legitimate network's SSID to lure users onto the attacker's AP.
Rogue access point
A rogue AP is an unauthorized AP plugged into your network. It doesn't have to impersonate anything.
MAC flooding
MAC flooding overloads a switch's MAC table so it floods traffic out every port.
VLAN hopping
VLAN hopping abuses trunking or double tagging to reach another VLAN. It's a wired-side attack.

quiz.q: A user can ping the default gateway and 8.8.8.8, but can't open any website by name. What is the MOST likely problem?
o: DNS resolution
Right. IP connectivity works all the way to the internet, so the name-to-IP step is what's failing.
The default gateway is wrong
With a wrong gateway, pinging 8.8.8.8 would fail too.
DHCP scope exhaustion
The PC clearly has a working IP configuration. Pool exhaustion would leave it with no lease or an APIPA address.
A bad patch cable
A bad cable would break the pings as well.

quiz.q: A new fiber link between two switches shows no link light. Both transceivers are the correct type and the cable passed testing. What should the technician check FIRST?
o: Whether TX and RX are transposed
Right. If the transmit and receive strands are swapped, neither side hears the other, so no link comes up.
Duplex settings
A duplex mismatch causes errors and slow performance on a link that is already up. It doesn't stop the link.
MTU size
An MTU mismatch causes dropped large packets after the link is up.
VLAN assignment
A VLAN problem affects traffic on a working link. It doesn't stop the light from coming on.

quiz.q: Each morning, early arrivals connect fine, but later users get 169.254.x.x addresses and can't reach anything. What is the MOST likely cause?
o: The DHCP address pool is exhausted
Right. Once every lease in the scope is taken, later clients fall back to APIPA. Shorten lease times or enlarge the scope.
The DNS server is down
DNS doesn't hand out addresses. Clients would still get valid IPs.
A spanning tree loop
A loop would hit everyone, early arrivals included, with a broadcast storm.
A rogue DHCP server
A rogue server hands out wrong addresses, not 169.254 addresses.

pbqs.title: Split the network into four subnets
pbqs.scenario: Your station was given 192.168.10.0/24. Split it into four equal subnets, one per department. Fill in each subnet's network ID, broadcast address and subnet mask.

rows.why: Four equal subnets means borrowing 2 bits: /26, mask 255.255.255.192, blocks of 64. The first block runs .0 to .63.
The next block of 64 starts at .64 and ends at .127, its broadcast.
The last block is .192 to .255. Every subnet keeps the same /26 mask.

pbqs.title: Diagnose six network tickets
pbqs.scenario: The help desk escalated six tickets. Read the output in each one and pick the cause. Each answer is used once; two options are distractors.

items.log:
Switch Gi1/0/7:  full-duplex, 1000 Mb/s
Server NIC:      half-duplex, 100 Mb/s
late collisions: 1,904 and rising
items.why: One side is full duplex, the other half. Late collisions are the classic sign of a duplex mismatch.

items.log:
Gi1/0/12 is up, line protocol is up
input errors 5,233   CRC 5,190   (rising)
note: cable run passes the generator room
items.why: Rising CRC errors on a link that's up point to a damaged cable or electrical interference along the run.

items.log:
IPv4 Address . . : 10.30.4.18
Subnet Mask . . : 255.255.255.0
User should be on Staff (10.10.4.0/24); can't reach the file share
items.why: The PC got an address from the guest range, so its switch port is in the wrong VLAN.

items.log:
IPv4 Address . . : 10.10.20.55
Subnet Mask . . : 255.255.255.0
Default Gateway : 10.10.21.1
Local printers work; nothing off the subnet does
items.why: 10.10.21.1 isn't inside 10.10.20.0/24, so traffic leaving the subnet has nowhere to go.

items.log:
Gi1/0/22: inline power denied, insufficient power budget
New camera on Gi1/0/22 never powers on
items.why: The switch has run out of PoE budget, so the new camera gets no power.

items.log:
> nslookup intranet
Server: 10.10.20.9
*** Request to 10.10.20.9 timed out
> ping 10.10.20.40   (intranet's IP)
Reply from 10.10.20.40: time<1ms
items.why: The host itself is reachable by IP; only name lookups fail, so DNS is misconfigured or unreachable.
